description: We are an interdisciplinary team of hardware/electronics engineers, AI developers, and full-stack/UI-UX designers. We are building an innovative AI-powered hardware and software solution for space exploration using NASA open data. Our team roster is already formed and ready for the hackathon!
summary: Stellanova is a browser-based health self-assessment dashboard that helps astronauts track and understand their own health during long-duration missions. On missions far from Earth, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in their own health, since real-time ground support may not be available. Stellanova lets a crew member log key indicators — heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood, fatigue, activity, and radiation dose — through simple manual check-ins, and view them against NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, distance from Earth, and hostile closed environments. An interactive hazards explorer and measurement guide explain why each indicator matters and which tool is appropriate for each signal. All data stays in the browser, so the tool works without a live connection to Earth. The current prototype uses manual self-reported input; our team’s next step is to pair it with dedicated sensor hardware for automatic data collection, which we began designing but could not complete within the hackathon timeframe. Stellanova demonstrates how a clear, explainable interface can support astronaut self-awareness and timely action, informed by NASA’s Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor project.
details:
What it does and how it works: Stellanova is a static, browser-based dashboard (HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, no backend) where an astronaut logs manual health readings — heart rate, blood pressure, glucose with meal context, body temperature, sleep, activity, and radiation dose — through a simple “Add reading” form, and completes a short daily check-in covering mood and fatigue. A deterministic health-assessment engine classifies each reading against configurable training-rule bands, treats missing or stale data as unassessed rather than assuming it’s normal, and gives urgent-symptom checks precedence over routine numbers. All data is stored locally in the browser (no account, no server), so the tool keeps working even without a connection to Earth.

Benefits: It gives astronauts a structured, low-effort habit for self-monitoring without requiring medical training, real sensor hardware, or constant ground support — directly addressing the challenge’s premise that astronauts “carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves.”

Intended impact: A foundation that could later connect to real wearable/sensor data and flight-surgeon-reviewed thresholds, starting from an interface astronauts can actually use and trust because it explains its reasoning rather than acting as a black box.

Creativity: Instead of a generic vitals dashboard, Stellanova organizes the entire experience around NASA’s own five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation/confinement, altered gravity, distance from Earth, hostile closed environment), pairing each hazard with plain-language explanations and a guide to which measurement tool fits which signal — directly answering the challenge’s own question of “which measurements can be performed in space.”

Factors considered: Communication delay with Earth (local-first, offline-capable design), the risk of over-trusting unvalidated thresholds (everything is labeled as training/demonstration data, not clinical diagnosis), and accessibility for crew members without a medical background.

Tools/technologies used: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, Node.js test runner for automated tests, Vercel for hosting, locally-hosted DM Sans and Manrope fonts (Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License). AI coding assistance (OpenAI Codex) was used during development; AI-generated imagery is labeled “Created by our team using AI tools” directly in the interface.
